header:
Date: 2025-08-12
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Emma Liu (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Javier Morales (Celestia Head of ML), Priya Singh (Platform Eng), Alan Brooks (CISO)
Notes: Discovery focused on cost/unit economics across Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments; batching/caching levers, budget constraints, security requirements and next steps.
transcript:
[00:00] Emma (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining \u0000 quick check, can you all hear me?
[00:03] Javier (Celestia): Yep, loud and clear.
[00:06] Marcus (Redwood SE): Hi all, Marcus here from infra, happy to dig into perf details.
[00:10] Priya: Great, thanks. We wanted to focus this session on economics mostly \u0000 token costs, batching, and how that changes between hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:18] Emma: Perfect. Quick agenda: run through current stack and volume, show Redwood pricing models at high level, Marcus will explain batching/caching levers and quantization impacts, then Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:27] Javier: Yep. Our context \u0000 we're a fintech doing customer-facing chat and automated report generation. Current stack is a mix: internal LLM for embeddings, but for generation we've been using a mix of hosted APIs (we have Pilot with a couple of providers) and some on-prem models for sensitive flows. Volume: roughly 10M tokens/week across prod and staging, with spikes up to 2x.
[00:45] Emma: Nice. Any hard budget constraint we should know about?
[00:48] Javier: We're targeting sub-$0.002 per generated token on average, that would keep the team within budget. Can you get there?
[00:55] Marcus: There's a couple of levers. Hosted is simplest \u0000 per-token pricing and no infra ops \u0000 but you pay the hosted per-token rate. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity that reduces unit cost for steady high throughput. Private \u0000 VPC/on-prem \u0000 shifts to licensing + infra costs, so unit economics depend on your infra amortization and utilization.
[01:12] Priya: For dedicated, how do you calculate unit costs? Is it just GPU hours divided by tokens?
[01:17] Marcus: Roughly yes, but we model it more precisely: cost = (reserved GPU cost + support/license) / usable tokens over time, and then we add smaller infra overheads. Important part is utilization assumptions \u0000 if you underutilize dedicated, per-token cost goes up fast.
[01:31] Javier: What about batching and KV/prefix caching? We have a lot of similar prompts and a few long-context flows.
[01:36] Marcus: Great question. Batching reduces the effective per-token compute by aggregating requests for the same model step. Continuous batching in the runtime can drop per-token GPU time by 20-60% depending on request distribution. Prefix/KV caching helps long-context use cases \u0000 if prompts share prefixes, the KV cache avoids recomputing attention for prefix tokens. That can be big for report generation where intro paragraphs are similar.
[01:55] Emma: To map that to cost: hosted pricing often assumes a baseline per-token rate; but when we run batching/caching heuristics on our end for dedicated/private, you can see much lower unit cost even at higher latency SLOs.
[02:07] Alan (CISO): Security question \u0000 if we do dedicated, what about data-in-transit, KMS, and audit logs?
[02:12] Emma: Dedicated includes network isolation between customers and option for customer-managed KMS. We provide audit logs, and for Private deployments you can use your own HSM. We'll share SOC2 and our security brief.
[02:21] Javier: Can you give a concrete worked example? Say 1M tokens/day, 30% caching benefit and batching that reduces compute by 40%.
[02:31] Marcus: Sure, quick back-of-envelope. Hosted example: if hosted is $0.004/token, 1M tokens/day = $4,000/day. But hosted has some economies at scale tiers \u0000 we can push lower for committed volume. Dedicated: assuming a reserved pool that supports peak throughput \u0000 the amortized GPU + infra + support might work out to $0.0009\u0001$0.0015 per token at 80% utilization. Apply caching (30%) and batching (40%) multiplicative-ish \u0000 effective compute tokens are lower, so you could hit sub-$0.0006 per delivered token in best cases.
[03:02] Priya: That range is a big variance. How do you prove assumptions? We need real benchmarks with our prompt set.
[03:10] Marcus: Exactly \u0000 we recommend a benchmark run: you give sample prompts and token distribution, we run 1M token synthetic/realized run across hosted and dedicated configs and show latency, cost and utilization.
[03:20] Emma: We'll also show sensitivity: if utilization drops to 50% the per-token for dedicated jumps. So we'll put a utilization curve on the pricing examples we send.
[03:29] Javier: About quantization \u0000 we've seen some providers talk about 4-bit stuff. What's the impact on latency and quality?
[03:34] Marcus: Quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput on some kernels. 4-bit or 8-bit can give 1.2\u00012x throughput gains depending on model and hardware. Quality impact is model-dependent; we recommend evals with your prompt set. For some models quantized variants are effectively indistinguishable; for others you see slight drop on edge cases.
[03:50] Priya: Private/on-prem \u0000 we have regulatory customers who can't send data off-net. How much does the economics change if we self-host in our racks?
[03:59] Marcus: It becomes capex and ops. If you have high utilization and spare capacity, self-hosting can be cost-effective. But you need to factor in ops headcount, hardware refresh, power/network, and for GPUs the procurement lead time. We can help with sizing templates.
[04:13] Alan: SOC2 and audit logs \u0000 will we get full access logs for all inference requests?
[04:18] Emma: Yes, we provide request-level logs for Dedicated and Private with redacted content options. For Hosted we provide aggregated logs and token-level metrics; request-level logs can be arranged under contract.
[04:28] Speaker 1: Sorry quick interruption \u0000 can you explain token accounting again? We sometimes count input+output vs only output.
[04:34] Marcus: Standard practice is to account both input + output tokens for per-token billing. We surface both in the console so you see breakdowns and can attribute cost to specific routes.
[04:43] Javier: On budgets \u0000 we have a hard monthly cap that can't be exceeded. Can Redwood support programmatic spend limits per route or per API key?
[04:50] Emma: Yes \u0000 rate and spend limits per API key, per customer org. For Dedicated we also support quota gates and alerts on utilization. We'll share examples of how customers have staged rollouts with spend guards.
[05:02] Priya: About fallbacks \u0000 if dedicated is saturated, can requests route to hosted fallback?
[05:07] Marcus: Yes \u0000 smart routing can fall back to hosted or different regions. That typically increases unit cost but maintains availability. It's configurable per route and per SLA.
[05:15] Javier: Any hidden fees? Like data egress or request count surcharges?
[05:19] Emma: For Hosted it's primarily token-based and embeddings have their own unit. There are optional add-ons like extended observability retention and compliance packs. For Dedicated you have the reserved capacity fee and any data egress depends on your infra \u0000 we call out all pieces in the pricing doc.
[05:32] Priya: We saw other vendors do dev/prod separation by model variants to save cost. Does Redwood support model variant pinning and automatic rollbacks if quality regresses?
[05:40] Marcus: Yes \u0000 rollouts, canary, A/B and automatic fallbacks are in the console. You can pin routes to model versions and configure health checks based on latency and quality metrics.
[05:49] Javier: For our internal projections, what's a realistic per-token range to model between hosted and dedicated for a 10M tokens/week workload?
[05:56] Marcus: Hosted might be $0.002\u00012$0.003/token unless you negotiate committed volume discounts. Dedicated amortized can be $0.0007\u00012$0.0015 at good utilization. With caching/batching applied you might model delivered cost at $0.0005\u00012$0.0012.
[06:10] Emma: We'll include low/median/high scenarios in the pricing deck.
[06:13] Priya: About benchmarks \u0000 can Redwood run them in our VPC for Private or do you need sample data?
[06:18] Marcus: For Private, we can run the same runtime in your VPC with a small on-site agent and do the benchmark. For hosted/dedicated we can run synthetic tests that mimic your distribution. We'll need the prompt set and a small script.
[06:28] Javier: How long does a pilot usually take?
[06:31] Emma: Typically a 4-week pilot to test perf and cost assumptions: week 1 ingest prompts & setup, week 2 run benchmarks, week 3 evaluate quality/regression, week 4 iterate and produce final cost model.
[06:41] Speaker 2 (Customer): Do you support per-route caching TTLs?
[06:45] Marcus: Yes \u0000 caching policies can be per-route with TTL and eviction strategies. We also support prefix-based caching for shared prompts.
[06:51] Priya: If we do dedicated, what's the minimum commit?
[06:54] Emma: Minimum depends on GPU class and region \u0000 we'll include examples but often customers start with a monthly reserved pool equivalent to a few GPUs. We also offer burst capacity for spikes.
[07:03] Javier: Back to token math \u0000 what's the sensitivity if we increase the average generated tokens per session from 100 to 300?
[07:08] Marcus: Linear on output tokens; but batching efficiency can improve with larger payloads if you can align request patterns. However latency SLOs matter: bigger outputs mean longer response times and more memory/KV usage.
[07:20] Emma: Also consider tokenization differences across models. We'll note model-specific tokens-per-word in the deck for your prompt set.
[07:27] Javier: On the security side, Alan asked about retention. We need to retain logs for 2 years and ensure PII is redacted.
[07:33] Alan: And we need proof of pen test and ISO/SOC compliance for legal.
[07:37] Emma: We can share SOC2 report and our pen test summary under an NDA. Retention is configurable \u0000 we can export logs to your S3 with lifecycle rules. PII redaction is supported via built-in redaction rules and customers can add additional processors.
[07:50] Priya: One more \u0000 for embeddings we plan to use a different route. Does embedding cost model differ?
[07:55] Marcus: Yes embeddings are billed per-embedding vector unit and have different compute characteristics. We can show combined examples in the deck.
[07:59] Javier: Any surprises we should be aware of when moving from hosted to dedicated?
[08:03] Marcus: The main ones: commit utilization risk, ops overhead, and model compatibility/quantization differences. Also some advanced kernels differ by GPU type which can change perf numbers slightly.
[08:13] Speaker 1: Quick logistics \u0000 who owns the PoC paperwork?
[08:16] Emma: I'll own it from the Redwood side; I'll send a pilot template.
[08:19] Priya: For the benchmark data, we'll scrub PII and send a 2k prompt sample by 8/15.
[08:25] Javier: Good. On the pricing examples \u0000 can you show a blended model where sensitive routes go to Private and the rest to Hosted?
[08:32] Emma: Absolutely. That's a common pattern \u0000 split routing by route tags, with private for regulated flows, dedicated for high throughput internal flows, and hosted for public-facing low-latency.
[08:44] Marcus: One more technical note: prefix caching effectiveness depends on token overlap. If your report intros are templated that's a big win; if prompts vary a lot, benefits are smaller. We'll measure that in the benchmark.
[08:58] Javier: Let's talk SLA \u0000 what's the latency SLO for hosted vs dedicated?
[09:02] Emma: Hosted typically targets p95 under 800ms for short prompts for curated models; Dedicated SLOs are configurable and tighter depending on reserved pools. We'll include actual numbers by model in the deck.
[09:12] Priya: Do you support model offloading to different GPU types to save costs?
[09:16] Marcus: Yes \u0000 smart routing can put less critical workloads on cheaper GPUs or older hardware; this affects latency but saves cost.
[09:23] Speaker 2: For the benchmark, do you simulate spikes?
[09:26] Marcus: We can run steady-state and spike simulations, and show how burst capacity and fallback affect tail latency and cost.
[09:33] Emma: Ok, rounding up \u0000 we'll send a pricing deck, pilot template, security docs, and schedule the dedicated sizing call. Any other immediate asks?
[09:41] Javier: Could you include an example of an invoice-level cost breakdown?
[09:44] Emma: Yes, we'll include a sample invoice with token breakdowns, reserved fees, and add-ons.
[09:48] Alan: Please include data residency options for EU and single-tenant control plane.
[09:52] Emma: Noted.
[09:54] Priya: One last question on monitoring \u0000 can we get token-level attribution to feature flags or product routes?
[09:59] Marcus: Yes \u0000 we instrument per-route and per-key metrics and can export traces to your observability stack.
[10:05] Javier: Great, thanks. That covers our main concerns.
[10:08] Emma: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and schedule the sizing workshop.
[10:12] Speaker 3 (off): Thanks all, bye.

[30:00] \u0001 meeting continues with some side technical clarifications and slower pace timestamps for remaining Q&A and light chatter \u0001
[32:15] Priya: We'll prepare the prompt set and the expected traffic profile and sync with Marcus.
[33:40] Marcus: I'll prepare a perf script and baseline numbers for both hosted and dedicated modes.
[34:50] Emma: I'll email the commercial examples and pilot template.
[36:10] Javier: Alan and I will review security docs as soon as they're available.
[37:00] Emma: Thanks again, we'll be in touch.
[37:10] Meeting ended.
